Title: Did John Coltrane ever play with Dizzy Gillespie? If yes, then what are some of the songs they played together and when did it happen?
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
+ 5
Sort
John Coltrane did indeed play with Dizzy Gillespie…and played with Diz’s bebop big band in 1949. There is a famous photo from Birdland, with Charlie Parker & Dizzy from 1950…which shows a young Coltrane in the background. This photo is sometimes cropped, and Trane is not shown in it. Coltrane recorded with Gillespie on some small group sessions from 1951. They were released on a small label…and can be found, if one wants to do the searching. Trane’s style in ’51 was more R&B flavored,due to Gillespie’s band orientation in those days. Bebop as a trend…was fading..and Diz had to make a living. That’s why the band’s repetoire consisted of novelty tunes,standards and of course, the blues.
Related questions
Related question
Who was the better musician: Miles Davis or John Coltrane?
Both musicians had different qualities, and both were excellent in their respective fields.
John Coltrane was a virtuoso with his instrument. His technique and improvisation were superior to almost any other jazz musician. He could play fast, and his improvisations could last as long as he wanted without being repetitive. He tried to push jazz beyond the limits in his final years with Free Jazz.
Miles Davis on the other hand, was never interested in how many notes per second he could play, he was more concerned on the tone, the emotion on each note and the space between each. When a new sub-genre was created, Miles would be one of the first to already be there.
So at the end, is to each listener to decide who he likes better, or maybe it’s not necessary to make that comparison at all.
Related question
Has Miles Davis ever played "Autumn Leaves" with John Coltrane?
Not that I know of, at least nothing that was recorded on an album. Miles DID record “Autumn Leaves” with Cannonball Adderley as a sideman on his Somethin’ Else record. And then when the 2nd Great Quintet was on the rise, it was a regular tune in his repertoire- though Coltrane was deep into his own group at the time.

However, it’s a pretty popular standard and it wouldn’t surprise me if they played it perhaps on a club date back in the 1st Quintet days. But nothing that’s been recorded on an official release to my knowledge. Wouldn’t surprise me in the least if it popped up on a bootleg with Miles and Trane. Plenty of recordings of “Autumn Leaves” done by both Miles and Trane, but not together thus far.
Related question
Who was the better musician: Miles Davis or John Coltrane?
Yes, really, what is the point of this question? Who was a better painter, Picasso or Dali? The better scientist, Newton or Einstein? The better godhead, Jesus or the Buddha?
Especially music is a domain of intuition and emotion and individuality. Miles could play fast and did so with Parker, but then repaired to a place he felt expressed his true nature better. It’s true that Miles drove himself through more phases and in that sense expressed more creativity in terms of many brilliant environments he immersed his horn in. But I mean, did you ever have two really good friends? Who was the better friend? They’re different, right? But both very cool people.
Your question is like, “What’s the best mountain, Everest or K2?”
Genius, especially artistic genius, is not quantifiable.

Related question
Was there an exact moment time when John Coltrane didn't have to look for work but instead other musicians wanted him to work with them?

In April 1957, Miles Davis fired John Coltrane for being an erratic, heroin-addicted liability. Less than a year later, Davis was actively pursuing Coltrane to win him back.
Before this reversal, Coltrane was a talented but struggling thirty-year-old journeyman saxophonist. He had spent years playing in rhythm and blues outfits and big bands, respected by his peers but far from a marquee name. While his initial break came in 1955 when Davis hired him to fill out a new quintet, Coltrane's addiction made him a liability on the bandstand, which ultimately led to his firing.
The exact moment the power dynamic flipped—when Coltrane stopped needing to hunt for work and instead became the musician everyone wanted to hire—can be pinpointed to the summer of 1957. Out of a job and at a personal crossroads, Coltrane returned to his family home in Philadelphia. He locked himself in a room, quit drugs cold turkey, and experienced a profound spiritual awakening that fundamentally altered his work ethic and approach to the saxophone.
Word of his intense new focus quickly spread, and a legendary composer took notice. Thelonious Monk personally recruited the newly sober Coltrane to join his quartet for a residency at the Five Spot Café in New York City starting in July 1957. This six-month gig served as the ultimate watershed moment in Coltrane’s career. Monk’s complex, idiosyncratic compositions pushed Coltrane to experiment with rapidly cascading notes and dense harmonic structures, a style that critic Ira Gitler would soon famously dub "sheets of sound."
The Five Spot residency became the talk of the jazz world. Musicians flocked to the club night after night specifically to study what Coltrane was doing. By the end of 1957, Coltrane was no longer an unpredictable sideman looking for a paycheck. The same Miles Davis who had fired him earlier that year asked him to return to a newly expanded sextet. Coltrane accepted the offer, stepping into the studio to record landmark albums like Milestones and Kind of Blue as a star in his own right, before ultimately commanding his own iconic quartet in the 1960s.
Related question
Did John Coltrane ever play with Miles Davis? Why did he start his own group?

You should do your research before asking such questions. Miles Davis hired John Coltrane in 1955, and except for a short period when Coltrane broke his heroin habit, the two played side by side until 1960. You can hear them together on the albums “Miles”, “Cookin’”, “Workin’” , “Relaxin’” and “Steamin’” (all on Prestige) and “Round Midnight”, “Milestones”, “Newport 1958”, “Jazz Track”, and the absolutely essential “Kind of Blue”.
Like many other musicians, Coltrane found musical concepts that he wanted to explore (particularly the modal style featured on “Milestones” and “Kind of Blue”). He founded his own group in 1960 and that quartet eventually became one of the most influential groups in jazz history. There are many classic recordings of Coltrane during the 1960s, including “Giant Steps”, “My Favorite Things” (both on Atlantic), and the Village Vanguard recordings (all on Impulse).

John Coltrane did indeed play with Dizzy Gillespie…and played with Diz’s bebop big band in 1949. There is a famous photo from Birdland, with Charlie Parker & Dizzy from 1950…which shows a young Coltrane in the background. This photo is sometimes cropped, and Trane is not shown in it. Coltrane recorded with Gillespie on some small group sessions from 1951. They were released on a small label…and can be found, if one wants to do the searching. Trane’s style in ’51 was more R&B flavored,due to Gillespie’s band orientation in those days. Bebop as a trend…was fading..and Diz had to make a living. That’s why the band’s repetoire consisted of novelty tunes,standards and of course, the blues.

Related question
Who was the better musician: Miles Davis or John Coltrane?
Both musicians had different qualities, and both were excellent in their respective fields.
John Coltrane was a virtuoso with his instrument. His technique and improvisation were superior to almost any other jazz musician. He could play fast, and his improvisations could last as long as he wanted without being repetitive. He tried to push jazz beyond the limits in his final years with Free Jazz.
Miles Davis on the other hand, was never interested in how many notes per second he could play, he was more concerned on the tone, the emotion on each note and the space between each. When a new sub-genre was created, Miles would be one of the first to already be there.
So at the end, is to each listener to decide who he likes better, or maybe it’s not necessary to make that comparison at all.
Related question
Has Miles Davis ever played "Autumn Leaves" with John Coltrane?
Not that I know of, at least nothing that was recorded on an album. Miles DID record “Autumn Leaves” with Cannonball Adderley as a sideman on his Somethin’ Else record. And then when the 2nd Great Quintet was on the rise, it was a regular tune in his repertoire- though Coltrane was deep into his own group at the time.

But nothing that’s been recorded on an official release to my knowledge. Wouldn’t surprise me in the least if it popped up on a bootleg with Miles and Trane. Plenty of recordings of “Autumn Leaves” done by both Miles and Trane, but not together thus far.

Who was the better musician: Miles Davis or John Coltrane?
Yes, really, what is the point of this question? Who was a better painter, Picasso or Dali? The better scientist, Newton or Einstein? The better godhead, Jesus or the Buddha?
Especially music is a domain of intuition and emotion and individuality. Miles could play fast and did so with Parker, but then repaired to a place he felt expressed his true nature better. It’s true that Miles drove himself through more phases and in that sense expressed more creativity in terms of many brilliant environments he immersed his horn in. But I mean, did you ever have two really good friends? Who was the better friend? They’re different, right? But both very cool people.
Your question is like, “What’s the best mountain, Everest or K2?”
Genius, especially artistic genius, is not quantifiable.

In April 1957, Miles Davis fired John Coltrane for being an erratic, heroin-addicted liability. Less than a year later, Davis was actively pursuing Coltrane to win him back.
Before this reversal, Coltrane was a talented but struggling thirty-year-old journeyman saxophonist. He had spent years playing in rhythm and blues outfits and big bands, respected by his peers but far from a marquee name. While his initial break came in 1955 when Davis hired him to fill out a new quintet, Coltrane's addiction made him a liability on the bandstand, which ultimately led to his firing.
The exact moment the power dynamic flipped—when Coltrane stopped needing to hunt for work and instead became the musician everyone wanted to hire—can be pinpointed to the summer of 1957. Out of a job and at a personal crossroads, Coltrane returned to his family home in Philadelphia. He locked himself in a room, quit drugs cold turkey, and experienced a profound spiritual awakening that fundamentally altered his work ethic and approach to the saxophone.
Word of his intense new focus quickly spread, and a legendary composer took notice. Thelonious Monk personally recruited the newly sober Coltrane to join his quartet for a residency at the Five Spot Café in New York City starting in July 1957. This six-month gig served as the ultimate watershed moment in Coltrane’s career. Monk’s complex, idiosyncratic compositions pushed Coltrane to experiment with rapidly cascading notes and dense harmonic structures, a style that critic Ira Gitler would soon famously dub "sheets of sound."
The Five Spot residency became the talk of the jazz world. Musicians flocked to the club night after night specifically to study what Coltrane was doing. By the end of 1957, Coltrane was no longer an unpredictable sideman looking for a paycheck. The same Miles Davis who had fired him earlier that year asked him to return to a newly expanded sextet. Coltrane accepted the offer, stepping into the studio to record landmark albums like Milestones and Kind of Blue as a star in his own right, before ultimately commanding his own iconic quartet in the 1960s.
Related question
Did John Coltrane ever play with Miles Davis? Why did he start his own group?
texts.3:
You should do your research before asking such questions. Miles Davis hired John Coltrane in 1955, and except for a short period when Coltrane broke his heroin habit, the two played side by side until 1960. You can hear them together on the albums “Miles”, “Cookin’”, “Workin’” , “Relaxin’” and “Steamin’” (all on Prestige) and “Round Midnight”, “Milestones”, “Newport 1958”, “Jazz Track”, and the absolutely essential “Kind of Blue”.
Like many other musicians, Coltrane found musical concepts that he wanted to explore (particularly the modal style featured on “Milestones” and “Kind of Blue”). He founded his own group in 1960 and that quartet eventually became one of the most influential groups in jazz history. There are many classic recordings of Coltrane during the 1960s, including “Giant Steps”, “My Favorite Things” (both on Atlantic), and the Village Vanguard recordings (all on Impulse).

John Coltrane did indeed play with Dizzy Gillespie…and played with Diz’s bebop big band in 1949. There is a famous photo from Birdland, with Charlie Parker & Dizzy from 1950…which shows a young Coltrane in the background. This photo is sometimes cropped, and Trane is not shown in it. Coltrane recorded with Gillespie on some small group sessions from 1951. They were released on a small label…and can be found, if one wants to do the searching. Trane’s style in ’51 was more R&B flavored,due to Gillespie’s band orientation in those days. Bebop as a trend…was fading..and Diz had to make a living. That’s why the band’s repetoire consisted of novelty tunes,standards and of course, the blues.

Related question
Who was the better musician: Miles Davis or John Coltrane?
Both musicians had different qualities, and both were excellent in their respective fields.
John Coltrane was a virtuoso with his instrument. His technique and improvisation were superior to almost any other jazz musician. He could play fast, and his improvisations could last as long as he wanted without being repetitive. He tried to push jazz beyond the limits in his final years with Free Jazz.
Miles Davis on the other hand, was never interested in how many notes per second he could play, he was more concerned on the tone, the emotion on each note and the space between each. When a new sub-genre was created, Miles would be one of the first to already be there.
So at the end, is to each listener to decide who he likes better, or maybe it’s not necessary to make that comparison at all.
Related question
Has Miles Davis ever played "Autumn Leaves" with John Coltrane?
Not that I know of, at least nothing that was recorded on an album. Miles DID record “Autumn Leaves” with Cannonball Adderley as a sideman on his Somethin’ Else record. And then when the 2nd Great Quintet was on the rise, it was a regular tune in his repertoire- though Coltrane was deep into his own group at the time.

However, it’s a pretty popular standard and it wouldn’t surprise me if they played it perhaps on a club date back in the 1st Quintet days. But nothing that’s been recorded on an official release to my knowledge. Wouldn’t surprise me in the least if it popped up on a bootleg with Miles and Trane. Plenty of recordings of “Autumn Leaves” done by both Miles and Trane, but not together thus far.
Related question
Who was the better musician: Miles Davis or John Coltrane?
Yes, really, what is the point of this question? Who was a better painter, Picasso or Dali? The better scientist, Newton or Einstein? The better godhead, Jesus or the Buddha?
Especially music is a domain of intuition and emotion and individuality. Miles could play fast and did so with Parker, but then repaired to a place he felt expressed his true nature better. It’s true that Miles drove himself through more phases and in that sense expressed more creativity in terms of many brilliant environments he immersed his horn in. But I mean, did you ever have two really good friends? Who was the better friend? They’re different, right? But both very cool people.
Your question is like, “What’s the best mountain, Everest or K2?”
Genius, especially artistic genius, is not quantifiable.

Was there an exact moment time when John Coltrane didn't have to look for work but instead other musicians wanted him to work with them?

In April 1957, Miles Davis fired John Coltrane for being an erratic, heroin-addicted liability. Less than a year later, Davis was actively pursuing Coltrane to win him back.
Before this reversal, Coltrane was a talented but struggling thirty-year-old journeyman saxophonist. He had spent years playing in rhythm and blues outfits and big bands, respected by his peers but far from a marquee name. While his initial break came in 1955 when Davis hired him to fill out a new quintet, Coltrane's addiction made him a liability on the bandstand, which ultimately led to his firing.
The exact moment the power dynamic flipped—when Coltrane stopped needing to hunt for work and instead became the musician everyone wanted to hire—can be pinpointed to the summer of 1957. Out of a job and at a personal crossroads, Coltrane returned to his family home in Philadelphia. He locked himself in a room, quit drugs cold turkey, and experienced a profound spiritual awakening that fundamentally altered his work ethic and approach to the saxophone.
Word of his intense new focus quickly spread, and a legendary composer took notice. Thelonious Monk personally recruited the newly sober Coltrane to join his quartet for a residency at the Five Spot Café in New York City starting in July 1957. This six-month gig served as the ultimate watershed moment in Coltrane’s career. Monk’s complex, idiosyncratic compositions pushed Coltrane to experiment with rapidly cascading notes and dense harmonic structures, a style that critic Ira Gitler would soon famously dub "sheets of sound."
The Five Spot residency became the talk of the jazz world. Musicians flocked to the club night after night specifically to study what Coltrane was doing. By the end of 1957, Coltrane was no longer an unpredictable sideman looking for a paycheck. The same Miles Davis who had fired him earlier that year asked him to return to a newly expanded sextet. Coltrane accepted the offer, stepping into the studio to record landmark albums like Milestones and Kind of Blue as a star in his own right, before ultimately commanding his own iconic quartet in the 1960s.
Related question
Did John Coltrane ever play with Miles Davis? Why did he start his own group?

You should do your research before asking such questions. Miles Davis hired John Coltrane in 1955, and except for a short period when Coltrane broke his heroin habit, the two played side by side until 1960. You can hear them together on the albums “Miles”, “Cookin’”, “Workin’” , “Relaxin’” and “Steamin’” (all on Prestige) and “Round Midnight”, “Milestones”, “Newport 1958”, “Jazz Track”, and the absolutely essential “Kind of Blue”.
Like many other musicians, Coltrane found musical concepts that he wanted to explore (particularly the modal style featured on “Milestones” and “Kind of Blue”). He founded his own group in 1960 and that quartet eventually became one of the most influential groups in jazz history. There are many classic recordings of Coltrane during the 1960s, including “Giant Steps”, “My Favorite Things” (both on Atlantic), and the Village Vanguard recordings (all on Impulse).

Dylan DeFeo's answer to Which Jazz musician do you prefer more, and why: John Coltrane or Miles Davis?

Granted, the link above is from more of a subjective question but it highlights the main point I wanna bring to this answer- you can’t really compare the two. We can’t weigh who’s better creatively; we can’t compare technique because sax and trumpet demand different techniques; influence is a difficult thing to measure especially with two titans such as Miles and Trane in which influences in certain respects can be disparate; and productivity isn’t necessarily the measure of good musicianship. There are some legendary artists who only put out a small output.
It’s folly to try to compare the two purely on musicianship, and comparing them creatively will only lead to subjectivity. Miles liked to use space to his advantage, and Coltrane liked to fill space as densely as he could muster. Some people like one approach more than the other, but the fact that they both defined modal jazz with this dichotomy was tremendously influential, and many (myself included) see their stylistic differences as a very effective artistic contrast. Some people back then hated what Trane was doing in Miles’ band.
So it’s best, I feel, to just listen and enjoy and draw your own conclusions. We live in a culture too concerned with ranking and listing and hierarchy and not concerned enough with artistic messages and craft. Art is never a competition.

What is the history between Miles Davis and John Coltrane? Did they hate each other because they were competitive with each other musically?
They didn’t hate each other. John Coltrane played with Miles Davis in his band, if Davis did not like him, he would never ask him to play with him. Miles Davis was sorry to see him leave, but he also realized that someone with Coltrane’s talent would not be around forever.

Related question
What key is John Coltrane's notorious Giant Steps in?
You probably already know it switches between B, G and Eb, changing order in different ways a few times. The question is whether one of them has more importance to our ear.
I think it is in B, since the first chord AND the authentic cadence in the 7th bar is B, like a lot of similar ABAB form pieces (adding up to 32 bars total). This is the strongest argument in favour of B, but then there’s that last cadence.
E flat is the first chord of the B section AND the last cadence, and it DOES sound settled, which makes a very strong argument for E flat as the central key. If you think of it in Eb, then B (the strongest key of the first 8 bars) is the key of bVI (C flat, really), which is a closely-related key.
Honestly, even though I hear B as the strongest of the three keys, I would not get into an arm wrestle over it. I think he meant the chord structure to sound as if there was NO central key, so that B, G and Eb sound equally strong to us. That’s perfectly fine, in my opinion.

John Coltrane was a virtuoso with his instrument. His technique and improvisation were superior to almost any other jazz musician. He could play fast, and his improvisations could last as long as he wanted without being repetitive. He tried to push jazz beyond the limits in his final years with Free Jazz.
Miles Davis on the other hand, was never interested in how many notes per second he could play, he was more concerned on the tone, the emotion on each note and the space between each. When a new sub-genre was created, Miles would be one of the first to already be there.
So at the end, is to each listener to decide who he likes better, or maybe it’s not necessary to make that comparison at all.
Related question
Has Miles Davis ever played "Autumn Leaves" with John Coltrane?
Not that I know of, at least nothing that was recorded on an album. Miles DID record “Autumn Leaves” with Cannonball Adderley as a sideman on his Somethin’ Else record. And then when the 2nd Great Quintet was on the rise, it was a regular tune in his repertoire- though Coltrane was deep into his own group at the time.
texts.1:
However, it’s a pretty popular standard and it wouldn’t surprise me if they played it perhaps on a club date back in the 1st Quintet days. But nothing that’s been recorded on an official release to my knowledge. Wouldn’t surprise me in the least if it popped up on a bootleg with Miles and Trane. Plenty of recordings of “Autumn Leaves” done by both Miles and Trane, but not together thus far.
Related question
Who was the better musician: Miles Davis or John Coltrane?
Yes, really, what is the point of this question? Who was a better painter, Picasso or Dali? The better scientist, Newton or Einstein? The better godhead, Jesus or the Buddha?
Especially music is a domain of intuition and emotion and individuality. Miles could play fast and did so with Parker, but then repaired to a place he felt expressed his true nature better. It’s true that Miles drove himself through more phases and in that sense expressed more creativity in terms of many brilliant environments he immersed his horn in. But I mean, did you ever have two really good friends? Who was the better friend? They’re different, right? But both very cool people.
Your question is like, “What’s the best mountain, Everest or K2?”
Genius, especially artistic genius, is not quantifiable.

Was there an exact moment time when John Coltrane didn't have to look for work but instead other musicians wanted him to work with them?
texts.2:
In April 1957, Miles Davis fired John Coltrane for being an erratic, heroin-addicted liability. Less than a year later, Davis was actively pursuing Coltrane to win him back.
Before this reversal, Coltrane was a talented but struggling thirty-year-old journeyman saxophonist. He had spent years playing in rhythm and blues outfits and big bands, respected by his peers but far from a marquee name. While his initial break came in 1955 when Davis hired him to fill out a new quintet, Coltrane's addiction made him a liability on the bandstand, which ultimately led to his firing.
The exact moment the power dynamic flipped—when Coltrane stopped needing to hunt for work and instead became the musician everyone wanted to hire—can be pinpointed to the summer of 1957. Out of a job and at a personal crossroads, Coltrane returned to his family home in Philadelphia. He locked himself in a room, quit drugs cold turkey, and experienced a profound spiritual awakening that fundamentally altered his work ethic and approach to the saxophone.
Word of his intense new focus quickly spread, and a legendary composer took notice. Thelonious Monk personally recruited the newly sober Coltrane to join his quartet for a residency at the Five Spot Café in New York City starting in July 1957. This six-month gig served as the ultimate watershed moment in Coltrane’s career. Monk’s complex, idiosyncratic compositions pushed Coltrane to experiment with rapidly cascading notes and dense harmonic structures, a style that critic Ira Gitler would soon famously dub "sheets of sound."
The Five Spot residency became the talk of the jazz world. Musicians flocked to the club night after night specifically to study what Coltrane was doing. By the end of 1957, Coltrane was no longer an unpredictable sideman looking for a paycheck. The same Miles Davis who had fired him earlier that year asked him to return to a newly expanded sextet. Coltrane accepted the offer, stepping into the studio to record landmark albums like Milestones and Kind of Blue as a star in his own right, before ultimately commanding his own iconic quartet in the 1960s.

texts.3:
You should do your research before asking such questions. Miles Davis hired John Coltrane in 1955, and except for a short period when Coltrane broke his heroin habit, the two played side by side until 1960. You can hear them together on the albums “Miles”, “Cookin’”, “Workin’” , “Relaxin’” and “Steamin’” (all on Prestige) and “Round Midnight”, “Milestones”, “Newport 1958”, “Jazz Track”, and the absolutely essential “Kind of Blue”.
Like many other musicians, Coltrane found musical concepts that he wanted to explore (particularly the modal style featured on “Milestones” and “Kind of Blue”). He founded his own group in 1960 and that quartet eventually became one of the most influential groups in jazz history. There are many classic recordings of Coltrane during the 1960s, including “Giant Steps”, “My Favorite Things” (both on Atlantic), and the Village Vanguard recordings (all on Impulse).

Granted, the link above is from more of a subjective question but it highlights the main point I wanna bring to this answer- you can’t really compare the two. We can’t weigh who’s better creatively; we can’t compare technique because sax and trumpet demand different techniques; influence is a difficult thing to measure especially with two titans such as Miles and Trane in which influences in certain respects can be disparate; and productivity isn’t necessarily the measure of good musicianship. There are some legendary artists who only put out a small output.
It’s folly to try to compare the two purely on musicianship, and comparing them creatively will only lead to subjectivity. Miles liked to use space to his advantage, and Coltrane liked to fill space as densely as he could muster. Some people like one approach more than the other, but the fact that they both defined modal jazz with this dichotomy was tremendously influential, and many (myself included) see their stylistic differences as a very effective artistic contrast. Some people back then hated what Trane was doing in Miles’ band.
So it’s best, I feel, to just listen and enjoy and draw your own conclusions. We live in a culture too concerned with ranking and listing and hierarchy and not concerned enough with artistic messages and craft. Art is never a competition.

They didn’t hate each other. John Coltrane played with Miles Davis in his band, if Davis did not like him, he would never ask him to play with him. Miles Davis was sorry to see him leave, but he also realized that someone with Coltrane’s talent would not be around forever.

Related question
What key is John Coltrane's notorious Giant Steps in?
You probably already know it switches between B, G and Eb, changing order in different ways a few times. The question is whether one of them has more importance to our ear.
I think it is in B, since the first chord AND the authentic cadence in the 7th bar is B, like a lot of similar ABAB form pieces (adding up to 32 bars total). This is the strongest argument in favour of B, but then there’s that last cadence.
E flat is the first chord of the B section AND the last cadence, and it DOES sound settled, which makes a very strong argument for E flat as the central key. If you think of it in Eb, then B (the strongest key of the first 8 bars) is the key of bVI (C flat, really), which is a closely-related key.
Honestly, even though I hear B as the strongest of the three keys, I would not get into an arm wrestle over it. I think he meant the chord structure to sound as if there was NO central key, so that B, G and Eb sound equally strong to us. That’s perfectly fine, in my opinion.
